Simulate Time-to-Event Data from a Custom mrgsolve Output

Source: R/simtte.R
sim_tte_df.Rd

Applies inverse transform sampling to a data frame produced by an mrgsolve simulation that contains a survival probability column. This function is useful when you have a custom time-to-event model implemented in mrgsolve and want to generate event times.

Usage

sim_tte_df(
  dat,
  surv_var = "p11",
  id_var = "ID",
  time_var = "time",
  xdata = NULL,
  event_time_method = c("grid", "log_survival")
)

Arguments

dat

Data frame. Output from mrgsim containing at minimum columns for time, subject ID, and survival probability. Columns are resolved by name (not position).

surv_var

Character string. Name of the column containing the survival probability (probability of remaining event-free). Default "p11".

id_var

Character string. Name of the subject ID column. Default "ID".

time_var

Character string. Name of the time column. Default "time".

xdata

Optional data frame of additional covariates to merge into the output. Must contain a column matching id_var.

event_time_method

Character string. "grid" (default) or "log_survival". See "Event-time interpolation" below. Partial matching is allowed (resolved via match.arg).

Value

A data frame with columns:

sim_time

Simulated event or censoring time.

sim_status

Event indicator (1 = event, 0 = censored).

ID

Subject identifier.

Plus any additional columns from xdata.

Trajectory contract

dat must contain, for each subject, one ordered survival trajectory satisfying:

  • at least one row;

  • time values that are non-negative, finite, and strictly increasing within the subject, with no duplicates. Rows are not sorted automatically: unsorted or duplicated times raise an error rather than being silently re-ordered or resolved by row order;

  • survival probabilities in \([0, 1]\) (a small numerical tolerance of \(10^{-8}\) is allowed for floating-point/ODE solver noise: values outside \([0, 1]\) but within this tolerance are accepted and then deterministically clamped to exactly \(0\) or \(1\) before monotonicity checking and event-time selection; values further outside \([0, 1]\) are a hard error, never silently clamped or dropped). This clamping cannot change whether a subject is classified as an event or censored, because stats::runif() draws from \([0, 1)\): a raw value already below 0 and its clamped value of exactly 0 both satisfy \(value \le U\) for every achievable \(U\), and symmetrically a raw value already above 1 and its clamped value of exactly 1 both fail it;

  • survival that is non-increasing within the subject (checked on the clamped values). A trajectory that increases by more than the same \(10^{-8}\) tolerance at any step is rejected rather than silently repaired, because that pattern cannot arise from a valid survival function and usually indicates a data or model error; an increase within the tolerance is treated as numerical noise and accepted as-is (not further adjusted).

A trajectory is not required to start at survival = 1 or at time = 0: sim_tte_df() never invents an implicit \(S(0) = 1\) state. Whatever survival value is reported at the first observed time is used exactly as given (see "Censoring and event-time resolution" below for what this implies when that first value is already at or below the sampled threshold). Subjects may have different time ranges; see below for what this means for censoring.

Censoring and event-time resolution

For each subject, a uniform random variate \(U \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0, 1)\) is drawn, and the first reported time at which survival is at or below \(U\) is located. If the first reported observation already satisfies \(S(t_1) \le U\), that first time is returned as the event time; no earlier crossing is inferred, and this is identical for both values of event_time_method (there is no earlier reported point to interpolate from). What happens next depends on event_time_method: see "Event-time interpolation" below. Exactly one stats::runif(1) is drawn per subject regardless of event_time_method.

If a subject's trajectory never crosses \(U\), that subject is censored (sim_status = 0) at the last reported time in their own trajectory, i.e. max(time) for that subject, for both values of event_time_method. Because this censoring time is subject-specific, sim_tte_df() does not inherently represent a common administrative censoring cutoff unless every subject's trajectory happens to share the same final time — each subject's final observation time is effectively that subject's own censoring horizon. There is currently no separate end_time argument to sim_tte_df() itself; sim_tte provides one for its built-in Weibull/M-spline models by ensuring every subject's generated trajectory is extended to a common end_time (see ?sim_tte).

Event-time interpolation

event_time_method = "grid" (the default) resolves event times purely by grid-based lookup, not interpolation: the returned time is always one of the times present in dat for that subject, never a value between two reported times.

event_time_method = "log_survival" additionally refines a crossing that occurs strictly after the first reported observation: it assumes the hazard is constant between the two consecutive reported trajectory points surrounding the crossing, and linearly interpolates cumulative hazard (\(H = -\log(S)\)) between them accordingly. For trajectories whose hazard is genuinely piecewise-constant on the reported grid (e.g. this package's M-spline model; see sim_tte's "M-spline hazard carry convention"), this recovers the event time implied by that discretized hazard exactly. For trajectories generated from a continuously-varying hazard (e.g. the Weibull model with shape != 1, or a custom mechanistic model), it is an approximation whose accuracy improves as the reported time grid is refined. event_time_method never changes which subjects are classified as events vs. censored, and never changes the returned time for censoring or a first-observation crossing — it can only change sim_time for a crossing that falls strictly between two reported points, and the interpolated time is always within that interval (never before the earlier point, never after the subject's final reported time).

Reproducibility

sim_tte_df() draws exactly one stats::runif(1) per subject, in the order subjects are first encountered in dat (row order), not in ID-sorted order. With a fixed set.seed(), results are therefore reproducible for a fixed row order of dat, but reordering the rows of dat so that subjects are first encountered in a different sequence changes which random draw each subject receives, even with the same seed and the same set of per-subject trajectories. This is standard, unmodified R RNG behavior (a single shared random stream consumed sequentially), not a bug; sim_tte_df() does not currently use per-subject or per-ID RNG streams.

See also

sim_tte, which builds the Weibull or M-spline trajectory this function consumes. simtte_example_model loads a bundled mrgsolve model whose simulated p11 trajectory can be passed as dat. sim_tte_ode, for in-solver event detection with no separate trajectory step. add_censoring and add_interval_censoring, to post-process this function's output (call add_censoring() first if using both).

Examples

# Create a mock survival probability data frame (no mrgsolve required)
mock_dat <- data.frame(
  ID = rep(1:3, each = 50),
  time = rep(seq(0.1, 10, length.out = 50), 3),
  p11 = rep(exp(-0.3 * seq(0.1, 10, length.out = 50)), 3)
)
result <- sim_tte_df(mock_dat)
head(result)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   sim_time sim_status    ID
#>      <dbl>      <dbl> <int>
#> 1     1.31          1     1
#> 2     9.19          1     2
#> 3    10             0     3

# Custom column names
mock_dat2 <- data.frame(
  subj = rep(101:103, each = 50),
  tgrid = rep(seq(0.1, 10, length.out = 50), 3),
  surv = rep(exp(-0.3 * seq(0.1, 10, length.out = 50)), 3)
)
result2 <- sim_tte_df(mock_dat2, surv_var = "surv",
  id_var = "subj", time_var = "tgrid")
head(result2)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   sim_time sim_status    ID
#>      <dbl>      <dbl> <int>
#> 1     2.73          1   101
#> 2     6.16          1   102
#> 3     1.11          1   103
